items.title: S&P 4.10 standard deviations below its 50-DMA: most oversold since August 2015
items.idea: SPX fell 3.7% Friday, its 7th straight decline and 5th straight close in extreme oversold territory. It lost 8.61% in five sessions and is now up just 0.95% YTD, 11.6% off its high. At 4.10 SD below the 50-DMA, the last comparable reading was 25 Aug 2015.
items.angle: Aug 2015 was a flash-crash low that got retested in Feb 2016, not a V. The closest analog says expect a retest, not a straight line back to highs.
items.tweetA: 4.1 sigma below the 50-day. Last time: August 24-25, 2015. That low held, but only after a nasty retest five months later. Oversold tells you to stop selling. It doesn't tell you to back up the truck. $SPY
items.tweetB: The S&P gave back an entire year in five sessions: -8.6%, leaving it +0.95% YTD. Energy is +34.8% YTD over the same stretch. This isn't a market crash, it's a referendum on one trade. $SPY $XLE

items.title: Tech's second 7%+ drop in 12 days. The only precedent is March 2020
items.idea: Technology fell 7.11% to its lowest close since April 13. Two ≥7% sector drops inside 12 trading days has only happened once before: March 2020, which had three. NVDA fell 14% and alone accounted for 54 of the S&P's 265-point decline (~20%).
items.angle: One stock produced a fifth of the index's down move. This is concentration risk running in reverse, and index vol now depends on single-name news (the SEC inquiry).
items.tweetA: $NVDA alone cost the S&P 54 points of a 265-point drop. One company, 20% of the damage. Passive owners bought concentration on the way up. Friday was the invoice. $QQQ
items.tweetB: The only other time tech had two 7% down days within 12 sessions was March 2020. Back then the Fed cut to zero within days. This time the debate is whether the Fed hikes. Same tape, opposite reaction function. $XLK

items.title: Tech -24.7% from its high but only -0.7% YTD. Staples is the lone sector up
items.idea: Comm Services is -24.8% from its high and -15.5% YTD, more than 11 pts behind the next-worst sector. Energy still leads at +34.8% YTD and Staples is +17.8%, just 2.3% off its high and the only sector green on Friday. Across the S&P there was 1 new high vs 27 new lows, and 21.1% of Comm Services names hit 52-week lows.
items.angle: With Staples near highs and Energy +35% YTD, the market is pricing stagflation-lite, not a growth crash. That matches Capital Flows' point that services inflation is still accelerating.
items.tweetA: Leadership board, Nov 20: Energy +34.8% YTD, Staples +17.8%. Comm Services -15.5%. When the defensive and inflation sectors win together, the market is pricing stagflation, not recession. $XLE $XLP $XLC
items.tweetB: Tech went from fighting for the year's top sector to -0.7% YTD in about a month. A 25% drawdown erased only the gains, not the base. The longs aren't underwater yet, so there's still room to sell. $XLK

items.title: IG yields are above the S&P earnings yield by the widest gap since the early 2000s
items.idea: Per Torsten Slok (Apollo), investors are now paid more to own high-quality credit than equities, with far less volatility. The last time IG yields were this far above the SPX earnings yield was the early 2000s, i.e., the dot-com unwind.
items.angle: A negative equity risk premium against IG is a structural argument for credit over equities in 60/40 rebalancing. It's an allocator flow story, not just a valuation story.
items.tweetA: Buy IG and you get a higher yield than the S&P earnings yield, with a fraction of the vol. Last time that gap was this wide was 2000-02. Equities didn't bottom until the gap closed. $LQD $SPY
items.tweetB: Every pension rebalancing committee will see Slok's chart this quarter. If credit pays more than stocks for less risk, the marginal dollar moves out of equities. Valuation is about to turn into flows. $LQD

items.title: 33 trading days from the Oct 6 peak to a 10% correction, one of the fastest on record
items.idea: The S&P went from its Oct 6 peak to -10% in 33 trading days. Friday was only the 6th time since WWII that the index fell all five days of a week with at least four 1%+ drops (Bespoke).
items.angle: Speed matters more than depth. A correction this fast forces deleveraging (vol-control, CTAs, risk parity), and those flows reverse just as mechanically once vol stops rising.
items.tweetA: Six times since WW2: a five-day losing week with four drops of 1%+. Every one of those was a forced-selling week, not a fundamental repricing week. Mechanical selling ends when vol stops rising, not when the news gets better. $VIX
items.tweetB: Peak to correction in 33 sessions. The typical 10% correction takes months. Speed like this comes from leverage unwinding, not earnings being revised. Watch the vol-control funds' re-entry triggers, not the headlines. $SPY

charts.desc: 🔥 Bespoke: prior occurrences of five down days with 4+ drops of 1% since WW2 (red dots); fastest-correction chart from Bloomberg

items.title: The capitulation stat: five -1%, three -2%, two -3%, one -4% day in 12 sessions
items.idea: OddStats: across the past 12 trading days SPX logged five -1% days, three -2%, two -3% and one -4%. Over 65 years that cluster has been followed by strong forward returns, 'even the scary dates.' The S&P is also oversold for the first time since March.
items.angle: This sits against Pasquariello's caution that one bullish ingredient is missing. Breadth thrust plus a Fed pivot is the usual confirming signal, and neither is visible yet.
items.tweetA: Five -1%, three -2%, two -3%, one -4%, all in 12 sessions. Historically, the forward returns from that cluster are great. Historically, the Fed also wasn't debating hikes into it. $SPY
items.tweetB: The bullish stat everyone will post this weekend. The one that matters more: NYSE A/D line at its lowest since late 2025, and more than half of the Nasdaq 100 already in bear markets. Capitulation needs breadth to turn, not just price. $QQQ

items.angle: When sell-side 2027 targets are already low, the bar for a positive surprise is low too. Contrarians will treat that as fuel.
items.tweetA: More than half of the Nasdaq 100 is already in a bear market while the index is 'only' in a correction. The generals held up the line. Now the generals are $NVDA. $QQQ
items.tweetB: Consensus 2027 S&P expectations are already muted, and that was written before this week. Sell-side targets get cut after the low, not before it. Watch for the capitulation notes in early December. $SPY

items.title: Nvidia -12% on reports of an SEC accounting inquiry; Anthropic IPO briefly above $2T fully diluted
items.idea: Manan's week summary: NVDA fell another 12% on reports of an SEC accounting inquiry. Anthropic completed the largest IPO in history, briefly above a $2T fully diluted valuation before much of the enthusiasm evaporated (DSOTB: it slid toward the offer price premarket). The Nasdaq gave up its YTD gain and the S&P entered correction.
items.angle: An accounting inquiry at the index's biggest weight is a different risk class than a multiple de-rating. It hits the credibility of the AI capex revenue chain itself (customer financing, round-trip deals).
items.tweetA: $NVDA raised FY28 guidance to +75% growth this week and fell 12% anyway on an SEC accounting inquiry. When the market stops believing the numbers, raising the numbers doesn't help.
items.tweetB: Anthropic printed the largest IPO ever and briefly traded above $2T fully diluted, the same week the supplier at the base of the stack got an SEC accounting inquiry. The top of the stack got priced at the same moment the bottom got questioned.

items.title: Private marks don't face the daily test: Isomorphic $5B, Genesis AI $500M while publics reprice
items.idea: In the same week public AI names cratered, Isomorphic Labs raised $5B and Genesis AI (humanoid robots plus a foundation model) raised a $500M Series A at $3.5B, led by Khosla, Premji and Eclipse, with NVIDIA, AMD and Samsung participating. A GP told Manan their firm loosened ownership requirements to win allocations. His question: if one term sheet says $12M and another $50M, did the founder get 4x better, or did FOMO get 4x worse?
items.angle: Public-private valuation gaps close through down rounds and LP markdowns 2-4 quarters later. That's a watch on secondaries discounts and VC-heavy endowments.
items.tweetA: Nasdaq gives up the year. Same week: $5B for Isomorphic, $500M Series A for a humanoid startup at $3.5B. Public markets mark daily. Private markets mark when they need to raise again. The gap is the LPs' problem in 2027.
items.tweetB: 'Did the founder become four times better, or did missing out become four times more uncomfortable?' That's the whole late-cycle VC market in one sentence. Price matters, and it always comes back.

items.title: Everful: AI matching retailers to Chinese factories, on track for $100M annualized revenue
items.idea: Everful raised a $48.5M Series A (Vertex SEA & India, January Capital, Square Peg, Lightspeed) for AI that connects retailers and brands directly with Chinese factories. CEO Sisi Song (ex-JPM, Alibaba, Bessemer) says it's on track for $100M annualized revenue by year-end.
items.angle: AI-intermediated sourcing that cuts out trading houses works against tariff and decoupling policy. It shows demand for Chinese manufacturing finding new rails rather than disappearing.
items.tweetA: Washington wants decoupling. Meanwhile an AI startup connecting Western brands straight to Chinese factories is heading to $100M run-rate in about 3 years. The supply chain isn't leaving China. It's losing its middlemen.
items.tweetB: $100M ARR from deleting the sourcing agent. Every Hong Kong trading house and Li & Fung-style intermediary should read the Everful round as a threat.

items.title: DOL PERM rewrite: Schedule A for nurses eliminated, layoff look-back goes from 6 months to 2 years
items.idea: The DOL's overhauled PERM green-card rule (Federal Register 17 Nov, 60-day comment period) eliminates Schedule A, the fast-track for registered nurses, physical therapists and workers of 'exceptional ability'. It also extends the disqualifying layoff look-back from six months to two years.
items.angle: Nurses are the biggest Schedule A category. Cutting their fast-track squeezes hospital labor supply and supports healthcare wage inflation. Hospital operators' margins are exposed.
items.tweetA: The DOL just removed the green-card fast track for foreign nurses during a nursing shortage. Hospital wage bills are the second-order trade nobody's modeling. $HCA $THC
items.tweetB: Two-year layoff look-back on PERM. Any company that did an 'AI efficiency' layoff in 2025-26 just lost the ability to sponsor green cards for two years. AI restructuring and immigration policy are now colliding.

items.title: EB-5 extension draft tightens the terms; courts block DHS on student status and CPT; H-1B $100K fee reply due Nov 25
items.idea: A Senate Judiciary draft would extend EB-5 Regional Centers to Sept 2032 but raise the jobs requirement per investor from 10 to 15 and the capital-at-risk period from 2 years to 40 months. It could ride the Dec 11 funding bill. Separately, a Massachusetts court vacated the DHS rule ending 'Duration of Status' for F-1/J-1 students, and another court enjoined the CPT internship crackdown. The government's reply in the $100K H-1B fee appeal is due Nov 25; the fee stays blocked until the First Circuit rules.
items.angle: The courts keep slowing down executive immigration tightening. The talent pipeline (F-1 to OPT to H-1B) survives for now, which supports US AI labor supply.
items.tweetA: Courts are now the main brake on immigration tightening: Duration of Status vacated, the CPT crackdown enjoined, the $100K H-1B fee blocked. Watch Nov 25. The AI talent pipeline runs through the First Circuit.
items.tweetB: EB-5 extension draft: 15 jobs per investor instead of 10, and 40 months at risk instead of 24. Wealthy Chinese and Indian applicants will price that in fast, and the program's appeal falls exactly as US real estate needs foreign capital.

items.title: Copper -8% on the week as data-center moratorium talk hits the AI-metal trade
items.idea: LME copper fell as much as 4% intraday to its lowest since March, heading for an 8% weekly loss (7%+ over two days on the 3M contract). In September it traded near a record $15,000/t on data-center demand. Since the Democrats' midterm sweep, talk of nationwide data-center construction moratoriums has hit the demand story. Benchmark's Albert Mackenzie argues AI's share of copper demand was 'over-egged'.
items.angle: Copper became a leveraged AI proxy, so it now trades on AI headline risk rather than on mine supply. The moratorium risk (domestic) and Trump's overseas data-center tax threat (foreign) squeeze data-center buildout from both sides.
items.tweetA: Copper was $15K/t in September on the AI story. Now Democrats talk data-center moratoriums at home and Trump threatens to tax data centers abroad. When both parties attack the same capex line, the metal that priced it in has to give it back. $FCX $COPX
items.tweetB: Copper fell alongside the LLM token price index. Commodity markets now trade the price per million tokens. That's either peak financialization or a genuinely new demand signal, and I'm not sure which yet. $HG_F

items.title: The LLM token price index keeps falling, and copper is tracking it
items.idea: The Silicon Data LLM Token Expenditure Index (SDLLMTK) tracks usage-weighted price per million tokens across LLMs and keeps sliding. That reflects either providers cutting prices or users moving to cheaper models. DSOTB overlays it with copper, AI stocks and Anthropic, and all of them are falling together.
items.angle: Falling token prices are deflationary for lab revenue per unit, but elastic demand could grow total spend. The key question is whether token volume growth outruns price declines. A falling usage-weighted price index suggests mix shift to cheaper models, which is bearish for frontier-model pricing power.
items.tweetA: The usage-weighted price per million tokens keeps falling. 'Usage-weighted' is the key word: it means users are actively choosing cheaper models. That hurts frontier-lab pricing power right as one of them IPOs at a trillion-plus.
items.tweetB: Everyone tracks GPU prices. Few track the price per million tokens. It's the AI economy's CPI, and it's deflating. Deflation is great for adoption and brutal for whoever bet on margins.

items.title: UBS says buy the dip: record Yangshan premium, Shanghai inventories at multi-year lows, $15,500 by mid-2027
items.idea: UBS WM CIO attributes the drop to sentiment plus rising exchange inventories, not fundamentals. Mine supply keeps disappointing, treatment charges are deeply negative, and grid and electrification demand is robust. Shanghai inventories are near multi-year lows and the Yangshan cathode premium over LME hit a record this month. The forecast stays at $15,500/t by mid-2027.
items.angle: Physical tightness in China (record Yangshan premium) alongside a paper selloff in London is the classic setup for a physical-led bounce. It mirrors the oil divergence Commodity Context flags (Dated Brent back above futures).
items.tweetA: Copper and Brent show the same pattern this week: paper sells off on AI fear while physical tightens. A record Yangshan premium and Dated Brent flipping back above futures. Physical usually wins these arguments. $FCX $SCCO
items.tweetB: Negative treatment charges mean smelters are paying to process ore. That's how short mine supply is. An 8% weekly drop doesn't create new mines, it delays them. $COPX

items.title: UBS: metals basket -10% WTD. Watch for AI fear to morph into a broad growth scare
items.idea: UBS's Justinus Steinhorst: the Metals & Mining basket {UBXEMETL} fell another 2% Friday and 10% week-to-date. 'Watch for AI fears to morph into a broader growth scare across assets. Yields and commodities are starting to move that way.' Gold fell for a 5th straight session too.
items.angle: If yields fall with commodities, the selloff turns from a tech de-rating into a growth scare. Capital Flows says bonds aren't confirming yet, and that is the key divergence to watch.
items.tweetA: Gold down 5 straight sessions in an equity crash. That isn't a safe-haven failure, it's margin-call liquidation: you sell what you can, not what you want. $GLD
items.tweetB: UBS says watch yields and commodities for confirmation of a growth scare. Commodities have confirmed: copper -8% and metals -10%. Bonds haven't. Until the 10-year cracks, this is a positioning unwind, not a recession call. $TLT

items.title: Brent at ~$93 on a 'stale' Middle East recovery narrative while physical firms: Dated back above futures
items.idea: Brent fell another ~$3 to around $93/bbl on the consensus view that Middle East supply is recovering, plus tech risk-off. But the contango in the physical Brent CFD curve is correcting after a month of weakness, and Dated Brent is trading back above prompt futures. Rory calls the recovery narrative 'sanguine and increasingly stale' given heightened security risks.
items.angle: Paper and physical are diverging. Futures trade the equity risk-off; the physical barrel says supply is still tight. Funds selling crude to cover tech losses create the entry.
items.tweetA: Brent futures -$3 on the week. Dated Brent, the actual physical barrel, just flipped back above futures. Macro funds are selling crude to meet tech margin calls. The refiners buying cargoes aren't. $XLE $BNO
items.tweetB: The 'Middle East supply is recovering' story is now consensus, and Commodity Context calls it stale. Middle East exports are slowing and inbound tanker capacity is down steeply. The market priced a recovery the ships aren't confirming. $USO

items.title: Gasoline cracks fall to the 5-year average for the first time since the Iran War began
items.idea: US gasoline inventories are surging, pushing cracks below year-ago levels to the trailing 5-year seasonal average for the first time since the Iran War started. Jet fuel is building counterseasonally. Crude and diesel stocks remain very low, but diesel cracks hit the lowest since July on October distillate exports, and the Russia/India export recovery faltered this week.
items.angle: Lower gasoline prices are behind the UoM inflation-expectations drop (4.7%→3.7%, Boockvar). The consumer relief is real, but diesel is the weak link if exports roll over again.
items.tweetA: Gasoline cracks are back to normal for the first time since the Iran War started, and UoM 1-year inflation expectations fell a full point to 3.7% the same week. The pump is doing the Fed's work. Diesel is the risk: stocks are still very low and the export recovery just stalled. $VLO $MPC
items.tweetB: Jet fuel building counter-seasonally is the strangest line in this week's oil data. Either airline demand is softening into the holidays or refiners overproduced. Either way, watch $JETS guidance.

items.title: Managed-money crude length at its lowest since early July: 'plenty of kindling' for the next rally
items.idea: Delayed CFTC data confirms the scale of the recent spec selloff, with net Managed Money length in major crude contracts at the lowest since early July. Positioning was roughly flat in the latest week. Rory says positioning risk now tilts 'squarely to the upside.'
items.angle: Light spec length, physical firming and security risk make an asymmetric long-crude setup into year-end, especially if equities stabilize and the risk-off liquidation reverses.
items.tweetA: Specs are as short as they've been since July, Dated Brent is above futures, and crude and diesel stocks are at the bottom of the 5-year range. All it takes is one Hormuz headline. $XLE
items.tweetB: Everyone's de-grossing tech, and crude got caught in the same deleveraging. When forced selling ends, the most under-owned asset with the tightest physical market snaps back first. That's oil, not semis. $USO

items.title: Chinese crude imports set a fresh post-'Beijing Swing' high as Middle East exports slow and ballast capacity collapses
items.idea: Commodity Context reports Chinese crude imports at a new post-'Beijing Swing' high-water mark. Middle Eastern oil exports keep slowing and inbound ballast (empty tanker) capacity to the Gulf is steeply lower. Rory also discusses the lagged link between Hormuz export volumes and realized prices.
items.angle: China stockpiling at highs while Gulf loadings slow is strategic accumulation. Fewer ballast tankers heading in means future loadings drop with a lag, which supports tanker rates.
items.tweetA: Fewer empty tankers heading into the Gulf means fewer loaded ones coming out in 3-4 weeks. The supply cut is already sailing. Meanwhile China imports at a fresh high. Beijing is filling tanks while the West sells futures. $FRO $DHT
items.tweetB: Chinese crude imports at a new high in the same week Trump returns from Xi talks. Strategic stockpiling isn't a trade signal on its own, but it tells you what Beijing thinks about the next six months of Gulf supply.

items.title: Goldman's Pasquariello: financial conditions most restrictive in 18 months. Is the Fed about to get 'properly rough'?
items.idea: Tony Pasquariello's eight observations: what looked like a routine AI correction is exposing something more uncomfortable underneath. Financial conditions are at their tightest in 18 months. Hedge funds have aggressively cut exposure, which sets up a squeeze, but 'one important piece of the bullish argument remains missing.' The real question is whether the Fed runs a conventional hiking cycle or something much more aggressive.
items.angle: Equities may be pricing a hiking cycle that bonds aren't confirming (Capital Flows). If the Fed doesn't go 'properly rough', the light gross exposure is fuel for a squeeze.
items.tweetA: Financial conditions tightest in 18 months, and the Fed hasn't done anything yet. The market tightened for them. If the Fed reads FCI, the hike may already be done. $TLT $SPY
items.tweetB: Goldman says hedge funds de-grossed hard, which is the squeeze ingredient. The missing piece is a reason to re-gross. Light positioning is necessary but not sufficient. Watch Fed-speak after Thanksgiving. $SPY

items.title: Trump threatens a 'tremendous tax' on US companies building data centers abroad, with no rate, authority or date
items.idea: Trump: 'We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country.' He threatened a 'tremendous tax' but gave no rate, legal authority or enforcement method (Bloomberg). His own officials were hearing it for the first time (Guardian). The earlier policy targeted Chinese remote access to US chips via overseas data centers. This wording targets the location of construction instead. The narrow reading is a garbled restatement of the China policy, made just after his Xi talks.
items.angle: This threatens hyperscalers' overseas capex (Gulf, Malaysia, India, Nordics) and the sovereign-AI deals. Combined with domestic moratorium talk, data-center buildout now has political risk on both sides. Watch for a Treasury or Commerce text.
items.tweetA: Democrats float data-center moratoriums at home. Trump threatens to tax data centers abroad. If both happen, where exactly does the AI capex go? $MSFT $AMZN $GOOGL $META
items.tweetB: Trump's own officials heard about the data-center tax for the first time on TV. No rate, no authority, no date. The tax isn't real yet, but the uncertainty premium on every Gulf and Malaysia AI campus deal already is. $ORCL

items.title: Ukrainian strikes bring down the Kerch Bridge road section; rail section possibly crippled
items.idea: Ukrainian strikes brought down the road section of the Kerch Bridge and may have crippled the rail section, cutting a major Russian supply route into Crimea (Al Jazeera, via Pressure Point's 'Things happen').
items.angle: Losing the rail span pushes Crimea logistics onto the land corridor and sea. That raises Black Sea shipping risk premia, with knock-ons for grain and Novorossiysk crude exports.
items.tweetA: The Kerch Bridge road deck is down and the rail span may be crippled. Crimea now has to be supplied by land bridge and sea, and sea means the Black Sea. Watch Novorossiysk loadings and war-risk premiums, not just the front line.
items.tweetB: While everyone stared at $NVDA, Ukraine may have taken out Russia's main supply route into Crimea. Black Sea risk premia have been compressing all year. That just reversed. $WEAT

items.title: COP31 goes into overtime over a draft that leaves out fossil fuels entirely
items.idea: Nearly 200 countries are disputing a COP31 draft agreement that omits fossil fuels and leaves other issues unresolved, and talks have gone into overtime (Guardian).
items.angle: A COP text that can't even mention fossil fuels tells you how energy security has displaced transition goals since the Iran War, which favors upstream capex over renewables.
items.tweetA: Two years after 'transition away from fossil fuels', the COP31 draft dropped fossil fuels completely. Energy security beat decarbonization. Energy is +35% YTD and that's not a coincidence. $XLE
items.tweetB: COP31 can't agree to mention oil in a climate deal. Meanwhile data centers are the marginal new demand for gas turbines. Climate diplomacy is losing to compute. $GEV

items.title: EU and UK agree a post-Brexit relationship reset
items.idea: The EU and UK agreed to reset their post-Brexit relationship at a summit (Foreign Policy). Separately, an Indian national got 19+ years in US prison for orchestrating the failed Indian-government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York. In the House, Speaker Johnson postponed a floor rule and urged Republicans to show up before Democrats take control.
items.angle: A UK-EU reset that cuts trade frictions is a medium-term GBP and UK-domestic positive, at a moment when US policy volatility is pushing allies together.
items.tweetA: UK-EU reset deal lands the same week Trump threatens to tax US companies building data centers abroad. Allies are re-wiring with each other while Washington rewires against everyone. Long UK domestics, quietly. $EWU
items.tweetB: A US court just sentenced a man for an Indian-state-backed assassination plot on US soil, while Washington courts New Delhi as its China hedge. That relationship has more friction than the trade headlines show.

items.title: UoM: 1-year inflation expectations collapse from 4.7% to 3.7%, and wealthy stockholders now feel worse off
items.idea: Final November UoM rose 3.5 pts to 51.5. One-year inflation expectations fell a full point to 3.7% from 4.7%. Low- and middle-wealth consumers reported better finances on falling gas prices, while those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline, 'consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets.'
items.angle: The K-shaped economy is flipping: the wealth effect that carried the top-income spending is reversing just as low-income consumers get gas relief. Luxury and premium discretionary are exposed; dollar stores and Walmart benefit.
items.tweetA: The K-shaped economy just inverted. UoM says low-wealth households feel better (cheap gas) and the biggest stockholders feel worse (AI selloff). The top 10% drive about half of US spending. Watch luxury, not Walmart. $LVMUY $RL
items.tweetB: One-year inflation expectations fell a full percentage point in a month, from 4.7% to 3.7%. If the Fed was about to 'get properly rough', the consumer just took away half the reason.

items.title: October core retail sales +0.6%, double the estimate, with September revised up to +0.5%
items.idea: Core retail sales rose 0.6% m/m in October, twice the estimate, and September was revised up four tenths to +0.5%. Home Depot: big-ticket (> $1,000) comp transactions +4.5% y/y, led by power and appliances. 13 of 16 departments comped positive, and Pro outperformed DIY.
items.angle: Strong real activity during an equity crash argues against the growth-scare read. It supports Capital Flows' view that bonds won't confirm while services inflation is hot.
items.tweetA: Core retail sales doubled the estimate, Home Depot big-ticket comps +4.5%, freight +5.9% y/y. Equities are pricing a growth scare. The consumer is pricing an ordinary Tuesday. One of them is wrong. $XRT $HD
items.tweetB: Home Depot's strongest big-ticket category was power. Generators and electrical upgrades are the household version of the grid capex trade. $HD $GNRC

items.title: Cass Freight +5.9% y/y, partly driven by IEEPA tariff refunds
items.idea: Cass shipments rose 5.9% y/y and 1.7% m/m in October. Cass cites slow retail and industrial growth, holiday restocking and, 'to some extent, the IEEPA tariff refunds', but warns that elevated inflation, rising rates and the temporary nature of the refunds will cap demand. KC Fed manufacturing rose to 18 from 11, and October IP fell only on utilities.
items.angle: Tariff refunds are a one-time fiscal impulse flowing through freight data. Strip them out and the freight 'recovery' looks weaker, so expect payback in Q1.
items.tweetA: Freight +5.9% y/y, and Cass admits part of it is IEEPA tariff refunds. A court-ordered stimulus check to importers shows up as a freight recovery. Strip it out before you call the cycle. $JBHT $ODFL
items.tweetB: KC Fed manufacturing at 18, core retail at double the estimate, freight +6%. The data is running hot right as financial conditions hit an 18-month tight. That's the setup for a Fed that can't cut into a selloff.

items.title: Nvidia raises its FY28 outlook to ~75% growth, up from 70%, off a higher FY27 base, and the stock fell anyway
items.idea: Nvidia: demand is strong across 'hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments', plus 'increased support from our supply base'. The FY28 revenue growth outlook rises to ~75% y/y from 70%, off a higher FY27 base. Palo Alto also 'materially' raised guidance, saying AI is accelerating cyberattacks and pushing platform consolidation.
items.angle: Guidance up and the stock down double digits on the week means the market is discounting the durability of customer funding, not current demand. The SEC inquiry and Anthropic's IPO wobble feed that.
items.tweetA: $NVDA guided FY28 growth UP to 75% this week. The stock fell 14% Friday anyway. When good guidance can't hold a bid, the market is pricing the customers' ability to pay, not the supplier's backlog.
items.tweetB: Palo Alto says AI is speeding up cyberattacks and enterprises are consolidating vendors to keep up. AI capex has a defensive twin, and it doesn't depend on Anthropic's IPO multiple. $PANW $CRWD

items.title: Walmart: food inflation 1-2%, 11,000 rollbacks, best food share gains in three years
items.idea: Walmart calls its customer 'stable, resilient' after soft patches in April and June. It ran just over 11,000 rollbacks in Walmart US by end-Q2 and Sam's invested in fresh-food pricing, delivering 'food share gains that we haven't seen in about three years.' Food inflation in the quarter ran 1-2%, 'pretty normal to even low.' Housing: single-family starts rebounded to 864k from 831k, and multifamily rose to 445k (peak 643k in Nov 2022).
items.angle: Walmart taking share through price investment is a margin trade-off, and it's deflationary for grocery peers. Food inflation at 1-2% plus falling gas helps the disinflation case.
items.tweetA: Walmart: food inflation 1-2%. UoM: inflation expectations -1pt. Gasoline cracks: back to normal. Every consumer-price signal this week says disinflation, while the market debates Fed hikes. $WMT
items.tweetB: 11,000 rollbacks bought Walmart its best food share gains in 3 years. That share came from someone: Kroger, Dollar General, Target. Walmart is spending margin to take the whole aisle. $KR $DG $TGT

items.title: The AI repricing: equities broke 7,400, but bonds aren't confirming while services inflation keeps accelerating
items.idea: Capital Flows' video note argues the selloff is an AI-specific repricing, not a macro growth signal. Rates are telling a different story than equities as SPX breaks 7,400, and services inflation is still accelerating. It covers the Fed path, vol positioning and the 'AI risk curve' to watch into Monday's open.
items.angle: If bonds won't rally on a 12% equity drawdown, the Fed put sits further out of the money. That makes this a valuation reset with no rate cushion, which is worse for long-duration equities.
items.tweetA: S&P down 12% from the high and the long end won't rally. That's the scariest chart of the week. No flight to quality means no rate cushion. Equities are de-rating with no help from the bond market. $TLT $SPY
items.tweetB: Services inflation accelerating plus an equity crash plus bonds not rallying: that's what a market looks like when it believes the Fed is stuck. Stagflation risk is the conversation for the Thanksgiving week. $TIP
